```{r setup, include = FALSE}
library(nlmixr2lib)
library(PKNCA)
library(rxode2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

# Model and source

Chou 2022 builds an interactive generic physiologically based pharmacokinetic
(igPBPK) platform for estimating withdrawal intervals (WDIs) of veterinary drugs
in food animals. One flow-limited whole-body structure (plasma, liver, kidney,
muscle, fat and a lumped rest of body, with a parallel metabolite submodel, a
two-compartment gut and two-compartment intramuscular / subcutaneous injection
sites) is calibrated separately for three drugs in two species. Six models are
packaged, one per calibration, exactly as the authors fitted them:

```{r models}
models <- c(
  "Flunixin, cattle" = "Chou_2022_flunixin_cattle_pbpk",
  "Flunixin, swine" = "Chou_2022_flunixin_swine_pbpk",
  "Florfenicol, cattle" = "Chou_2022_florfenicol_cattle_pbpk",
  "Florfenicol, swine" = "Chou_2022_florfenicol_swine_pbpk",
  "Penicillin G, cattle" = "Chou_2022_penicillinG_cattle_pbpk",
  "Penicillin G, swine" = "Chou_2022_penicillinG_swine_pbpk"
)
uis <- lapply(models, function(m) rxode2::rxode2(readModelDb(m)))
```

* Citation: `r uis[[1]]$reference`
* Article: <https://doi.org/10.1093/toxsci/kfac056>
* Supplementary Data (equations S1-S22, tissue composition, dosing regimens):
  available with the article at the DOI above
* Authors' code and data (mrgsolve model, fitted parameters, digitised
  observations): <https://github.com/UFPBPK/FARAD-igPBPK>

Each model takes body weight `WT` (kg) as its only covariate. Doses are in mg
and go into `plasma` (intravenous), `stomach` (oral), `depot` + `depot2`
(intramuscular; for flunixin `depot` alone) or `depot3` + `depot4`
(subcutaneous; for flunixin `depot3` alone). For the two-compartment injection
sites the same amount is dosed into both compartments and the model's
bioavailability terms place the fraction `Frac` at the fast-absorption site
and `1 - Frac` in the slow-release depot. Concentrations are in mg/L (ug/g in
tissue).

# Population

No animals were dosed for this paper. Each drug-species model was calibrated
by weighted least squares against mean concentration-time data collected from
the Food Animal Residue Avoidance Databank (FARAD) Comparative Pharmacokinetic
Database, taken from tables or digitised from figures (Chou 2022 Table 1), and
evaluated against held-out studies. Data in dairy cows and lactating sows were
excluded. The number of studies per model is:

```{r population}
pop <- bind_rows(lapply(names(uis), function(nm) {
  p <- uis[[nm]]$population
  data.frame(Model = nm, Studies = p$n_studies, Doses = p$dose_range)
}))
knitr::kable(pop)
```

Individual animal counts are not reported. The withdrawal-interval
simulations use 300 kg cattle and 92 kg swine (the authors' code), with body
weight sampled normally (CV 20%). The full metadata is available as
`readModelDb("Chou_2022_flunixin_cattle_pbpk")()$population`.

# Source trace

Every `ini()` value carries an in-file comment naming its source. In summary:

| Element | Source |
|---|---|
| Two-compartment IM / SC injection sites | Supplementary Equations S1-S6; code `Rim`, `Rsiteim`, `ADOSEim` |
| Stomach and small intestine | Equations S7-S9; code `RST`, `RSI` (no stomach uptake K0 in the code) |
| Hepatic metabolism `Rmet = KmetC*BW*AL` | Equation S10; code `Rmet` |
| Enterohepatic reabsorption and biliary return of parent and metabolite | Equations S11-S13; code `RL`, `RSI` |
| Urinary excretion from kidney venous blood | Equation S14; code `Rurine` |
| Flow-limited tissue mass balance | Equations S15-S16; code `RK`, `RM`, `RF`, `Rrest` |
| Plasma state, `CPlas = CPlas_free/Free`, IV dose into `APlas_free` | deposited code `GenPBPK.R` (not written out in the supplement) |
| Flow and volume renormalisation | code `$MAIN` (`sumQ`, `sumV`) |
| Physiology (QCC, flow and volume fractions, Htc) | Table 2 |
| Chemical-specific parameters | Table 3 (cattle), Table 4 (swine); fitted values at the precision of the deposited `Fit_*.rds` |
| Gastric emptying GE = 0.182 /h | deposited code only |
| Monte Carlo coefficients of variation | Materials and Methods, 'Establishment of a population PBPK model'; Table 2 SDs |

The typical values of all six models side by side (back-transformed; `fixed`
marks values not fitted by the authors):

```{r source-trace}
ini_tab <- bind_rows(lapply(names(uis), function(nm) {
  d <- uis[[nm]]$iniDf
  d <- d[is.na(d$neta1) & is.na(d$err), ]
  d <- d[d$name != "propSd", ]
  val <- ifelse(startsWith(d$name, "l"), exp(d$est), d$est)
  data.frame(
    parameter = sub("_(5oh|floa|metab)$", "_met", d$name),
    model = nm,
    value = paste0(signif(val, 4), ifelse(d$fix, " (fixed)", ""))
  )
}))
ini_wide <- ini_tab |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = model, values_from = value, values_fill = "")
knitr::kable(ini_wide)
```

Here `_met` stands for the metabolite suffix: `_5oh` (5-hydroxyflunixin),
`_floa` (florfenicol amine) or `_metab` (the unnamed penicillin G metabolites).
Rate constants `lkreab` (KehcC) and `lkmet` (KmetC) and clearances `lcl_*`
are per kg of body weight. The values that depart from Tables 3 and 4, and
why, are listed under [Assumptions and deviations](#assumptions-and-deviations).

# Known-answer check against the authors' code

The authors deposited their mrgsolve model (`GenPBPK.R`). The maintainers ran
that code at the parameter values of these six models, for each model's
FDA-label dosing regimen at the Monte Carlo reference body weight, and
recorded the concentrations below. The packaged models must reproduce them;
both sides use identical parameters, so the difference is pure numerical error
and a tight bound is appropriate. In the authors' code the intravenous dose is
a 0.01 h infusion, so the same is done here.

```{r helpers}
# Label (FDA-approved) regimens of Supplementary Table 8, as the authors
# simulated them (Figure_5_6.R in the deposited code).
label <- data.frame(
  key = c("flunixin_cattle", "flunixin_swine", "florfenicol_cattle", "florfenicol_cattle",
          "florfenicol_swine", "penicillinG_cattle", "penicillinG_swine"),
  scenario = c("IV 2.2 mg/kg q24h x3", "IM 2.2 mg/kg x1", "IM 20 mg/kg q48h x2",
               "SC 40 mg/kg x1", "oral 14 mg/kg q24h x5", "IM 6.5 mg/kg q24h x5",
               "IM 6.5 mg/kg q24h x5"),
  route = c("iv", "im", "im", "sc", "po", "im", "im"),
  dose = c(2.2, 2.2, 20, 40, 14, 6.5, 6.5),
  n = c(3, 1, 2, 1, 5, 5, 5),
  ii = c(24, 24, 48, 24, 24, 24, 24)
)
model_of <- function(key) models[[match(key, sub("Chou_2022_(.*)_pbpk", "\\1", models))]]

# Dosing rows for one animal. Two-compartment injection sites get the full
# amount in both compartments; the model's f() terms split it.
dose_rows <- function(route, amt, n, ii, dissolution) {
  t <- (seq_len(n) - 1) * ii
  cmts <- switch(route,
    iv = "plasma",
    po = "stomach",
    im = if (dissolution) c("depot", "depot2") else "depot",
    sc = if (dissolution) c("depot3", "depot4") else "depot3"
  )
  d <- expand.grid(time = t, cmt = cmts, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  d$amt <- amt
  d$rate <- if (route == "iv") amt / 0.01 else 0
  d$evid <- 1
  d
}

# Event table for a cohort: one block per animal, observations on `plasma`
# (a state; the algebraic outputs come back at every observation row).
cohort_events <- function(wt, route, dose, n, ii, dissolution, obs_times) {
  bind_rows(lapply(seq_along(wt), function(i) {
    dr <- dose_rows(route, dose * wt[i], n, ii, dissolution)
    ob <- data.frame(time = obs_times, cmt = "plasma", amt = 0, rate = 0, evid = 0)
    out <- bind_rows(dr, ob)
    out$id <- i
    out$WT <- wt[i]
    out
  })) |>
    arrange(id, time, desc(evid))
}

has_dissolution <- function(ui) "depot2" %in% ui$state
```

```{r known-answer}
ka_check <- bind_rows(lapply(unique(ref$model), function(key) {
  ui <- uis[[match(model_of(key), models)]]
  lab <- label[match(key, label$key), ]
  wt <- ui$covariateData$WT$reference_value
  ev <- cohort_events(wt, lab$route, lab$dose, lab$n, lab$ii, has_dissolution(ui),
                      obs_times = c(2, 24, 72, 168, 336))
  sim <- rxode2::rxSolve(rxode2::zeroRe(ui), ev, atol = 1e-12, rtol = 1e-10,
                         maxsteps = 500000L, returnType = "data.frame")
  met_liver <- grep("^a_liver_", names(sim), value = TRUE)
  sim$Cliver_met <- sim[[met_liver]] / sim$v_liver
  r <- ref[ref$model == key, ]
  sim <- sim[match(r$time, sim$time), ]
  data.frame(model = key, time = r$time,
    max_rel_diff = apply(abs(as.matrix(sim[, names(r)[3:8]]) / as.matrix(r[, 3:8]) - 1), 1, max))
}))
knitr::kable(ka_check |> group_by(model) |> summarise(max_rel_diff = signif(max(max_rel_diff), 2)))
stopifnot(max(ka_check$max_rel_diff) < 1e-4)
```

All six models reproduce the authors' code to within the printed precision of
the reference values. `Cliver_met` is the metabolite liver concentration
(5-hydroxyflunixin, florfenicol amine, or the unnamed penicillin G
metabolites), so the metabolite submodels and their molar coupling are checked
too.

# Mass balance

The authors' code tracks amounts in mmol so that metabolism is mole-for-mole;
the packaged models track mg and convert with the molecular-weight ratio.
After a single dose every mole must still be somewhere: in the parent
compartments, in the metabolite compartments, or excreted (biliary metabolite
re-enters the gut as parent, so bile is not a sink).

```{r mass-balance}
# Molecular weights (g/mol) of parent and metabolite, Chou 2022 Table 3.
mw_tab <- list(flunixin = c(296.4, 312.4), florfenicol = c(358.2, 247.3),
               penicillinG = c(334, 334))
mb <- bind_rows(lapply(names(uis), function(nm) {
  ui <- uis[[nm]]
  mw <- mw_tab[[sub("Chou_2022_([A-Za-z]+)_.*", "\\1", models[[nm]])]]
  met <- sub("^plasma_", "", grep("^plasma_", ui$state, value = TRUE))
  wt <- ui$covariateData$WT$reference_value
  route <- if (has_dissolution(ui)) "im" else "sc"
  ev <- cohort_events(wt, route, 10, 1, 24, has_dissolution(ui), obs_times = c(24, 336))
  sim <- rxode2::rxSolve(rxode2::zeroRe(ui), ev, atol = 1e-12, rtol = 1e-10,
                         maxsteps = 500000L, returnType = "data.frame")
  parent <- setdiff(ui$state, c(grep(paste0("_", met, "$"), ui$state, value = TRUE), "a_metabolized"))
  metab <- grep(paste0("_", met, "$"), ui$state, value = TRUE)
  mol <- rowSums(sim[, parent]) / mw[1] + rowSums(sim[, metab]) / mw[2]
  data.frame(Model = nm, time = sim$time, recovered = mol / (10 * wt / mw[1]))
}))
knitr::kable(mb |> mutate(recovered = signif(recovered, 8)))
stopifnot(all(abs(mb$recovered - 1) < 1e-6))
```

# Withdrawal intervals: Monte Carlo replication of Figures 5 and 6 and Table 5

## Sampling as the authors did

The authors' Monte Carlo draws every parameter from a distribution truncated
at its 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles, and parameterises the log-normal ones so
that the arithmetic mean (not the median) equals the tabulated value
(`logM = log(M / sqrt(1 + CV^2))` in the deposited `Pars.R`). Neither feature
can be expressed as an `ini()` omega: the packaged models carry the tabulated
value as the typical value (median) and the authors' CVs as fixed variances.
To reproduce the authors' sampling exactly, the etas are drawn here directly,
truncated at |z| < 1.96 and shifted by `-omega^2/2` for the log-normal
parameters, and passed to the solver on a `zeroRe()` copy of the model. Body
weight is drawn from a normal distribution truncated at the same quantiles
(mean 300 kg in cattle and 92 kg in swine, CV 20%).

```{r mc-draws}
rtrunc_z <- function(n) qnorm(runif(n, pnorm(-1.96), pnorm(1.96)))

draw_animals <- function(ui, n) {
  om <- diag(ui$omega)
  etas <- vapply(names(om), function(e) {
    sd <- sqrt(om[[e]])
    z <- rtrunc_z(n)
    # log-normal parameters (etal*) are mean-preserving, normal ones are not shifted
    if (startsWith(e, "etal")) -sd^2 / 2 + z * sd else z * sd
  }, numeric(n))
  if (n == 1) etas <- matrix(etas, nrow = 1, dimnames = list(NULL, names(om)))
  wt0 <- ui$covariateData$WT$reference_value
  data.frame(id = seq_len(n), WT = wt0 * (1 + 0.2 * rtrunc_z(n)), etas, check.names = FALSE)
}
```

## Simulation

Each label regimen is simulated for 200 animals (the authors used 1000). The
withdrawal interval is the first time after the last dose at which the 99th
percentile of the tissue concentration falls to or below the tolerance,
rounded up to whole days. For florfenicol the marker residue is florfenicol
amine. Kidney uses the liver tolerance (Chou 2022 Methods).

```{r mc-sim}
rxode2::rxSetSeed(20220601)
set.seed(20220601)
n_animals <- 200

tolerances <- data.frame(
  key = c("flunixin_cattle", "flunixin_swine", "florfenicol_cattle", "florfenicol_swine",
          "penicillinG_cattle", "penicillinG_swine"),
  liver = c(0.125, 0.03, 3.7, 2.5, 0.05, 0.025),
  muscle = c(0.025, 0.025, 0.3, 0.2, 0.05, 0.025)
)

simulate_label <- function(i, theta_override = NULL) {
  lab <- label[i, ]
  ui <- uis[[match(model_of(lab$key), models)]]
  last <- (lab$n - 1) * lab$ii
  obs <- seq(0, last + 45 * 24, by = 3)
  draws <- draw_animals(ui, n_animals)
  if (!is.null(theta_override)) draws <- cbind(draws, as.data.frame(as.list(theta_override)))
  ev <- cohort_events(draws$WT, lab$route, lab$dose, lab$n, lab$ii, has_dissolution(ui), obs)
  sim <- suppressWarnings(rxode2::rxSolve(
    rxode2::zeroRe(ui), ev, params = draws[, names(draws) != "WT"],
    returnType = "data.frame", maxsteps = 500000L
  ))
  met <- if (startsWith(lab$key, "florfenicol")) "_floa" else ""
  tissue <- sim |>
    transmute(id, time,
      Liver = .data[[paste0("Cliver", met)]],
      Kidney = .data[[paste0("Ckidney", met)]],
      Muscle = .data[[paste0("Cmuscle", met)]]) |>
    pivot_longer(c(Liver, Kidney, Muscle), names_to = "tissue", values_to = "conc")
  tissue |>
    group_by(tissue, time) |>
    summarise(p01 = quantile(conc, 0.01), p50 = median(conc), p99 = quantile(conc, 0.99),
              .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(scenario = lab$scenario, key = lab$key, last_dose = last)
}

mc <- bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(nrow(label)), simulate_label))
```

```{r wdi}
wdi_of <- function(d) {
  tol <- tolerances[match(d$key[1], tolerances$key), ]
  out <- d |>
    mutate(tol = ifelse(tissue == "Muscle", tol$muscle, tol$liver)) |>
    filter(time > last_dose, round(p99, 3) <= tol) |>
    group_by(tissue) |>
    summarise(wdi = ceiling(min(time - last_dose) / 24), .groups = "drop")
  out
}
wdi <- mc |>
  group_by(key, scenario) |>
  group_modify(~ wdi_of(mutate(.x, key = .y$key))) |>
  ungroup()

table5 <- data.frame(
  key = rep(label$key, each = 3),
  scenario = rep(label$scenario, each = 3),
  tissue = rep(c("Liver", "Kidney", "Muscle"), times = nrow(label)),
  table5 = c(7, 2, 8, 13, 14, 4, 26, 15, 28, 35, 19, 39, 16, 10, 16, 7, 3, 2, 1, 11, 1)
)
wdi_cmp <- wdi |>
  left_join(table5, by = c("key", "scenario", "tissue")) |>
  mutate(species = sub(".*_", "", key), drug = sub("_.*", "", key)) |>
  select(drug, species, scenario, tissue, wdi, table5)
wdi_cmp |>
  rename("Drug" = drug, "Species" = species, "Label regimen" = scenario, "Tissue" = tissue,
         "WDI, this model (days)" = wdi, "WDI, Chou 2022 Table 5 (days)" = table5) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

```{r wdi-check}
# The 99th percentile of 200 animals is an extreme order statistic whose
# value changes with the random stream, so the check is on the centre of the
# paired differences across all 21 tissue-regimen pairs, not on any one pair.
stopifnot(abs(median(wdi_cmp$wdi - wdi_cmp$table5)) <= 2)
```

The intervals agree with Table 5 to within the Monte Carlo noise of a 99th
percentile estimated from 200 animals (rerunning the authors' own code with
different random seeds moves single intervals by about one day). Two
systematic differences remain and are explained under
[Assumptions and deviations](#assumptions-and-deviations): Table 5 was
generated with an earlier version of the authors' code, and the swine
flunixin model here uses the Table 4 absorption constants where that code used
others.

```{r figure-5-6, fig.height = 8}
plot_mc <- mc |>
  left_join(tolerances, by = "key") |>
  mutate(tol = ifelse(tissue == "Muscle", muscle, liver),
         day = (time - last_dose) / 24,
         panel = paste(scenario, sub("_", ", ", key), sep = "\n"),
         p01 = pmax(p01, 1e-6))
ggplot(plot_mc, aes(day, p50, colour = tissue)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_line(aes(y = p99), linetype = 2) +
  geom_line(aes(y = p01), linetype = 3) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = tol), linetype = 4, colour = "grey30") +
  scale_y_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  labs(x = "Days after the last dose", y = "Tissue concentration (ug/g)",
       colour = "Tissue",
       title = "Replicates Figures 5 and 6 of Chou 2022",
       caption = "Median (solid), 1st and 99th percentiles (dotted, dashed); tolerance (dash-dot). Florfenicol: florfenicol amine.")
```

## Effect of the swine flunixin absorption constants

For swine flunixin, Table 4 and the authors' calibration script use
Kim = 1 /h and Kabs = 0.4 /h (the values packaged here), but the figure and
web-application code that produced Table 5 use Kim = 0.5 /h and Kabs = 1.9 /h.
Rerunning the label regimen with the latter shows how much of the difference
in the swine flunixin row they explain:

```{r flunixin-swine-alt}
alt <- simulate_label(which(label$key == "flunixin_swine"),
                      theta_override = c(lka_im = log(0.5), lka = log(1.9)))
bind_rows(
  wdi_of(mc |> filter(key == "flunixin_swine")) |> mutate(values = "Table 4 (packaged)"),
  wdi_of(alt) |> mutate(values = "figure / app code")
) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = values, values_from = wdi) |>
  rename("Tissue" = tissue) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

# Noncompartmental analysis of the plasma profiles

Chou 2022 reports no noncompartmental parameters, so there is no published
table to compare against; the typical-animal plasma profile after a single
label dose is summarised with PKNCA as a reference for users.

```{r nca}
nca_sims <- bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(nrow(label)), function(i) {
  lab <- label[i, ]
  ui <- uis[[match(model_of(lab$key), models)]]
  wt <- ui$covariateData$WT$reference_value
  ev <- cohort_events(wt, lab$route, lab$dose, 1, lab$ii, has_dissolution(ui),
                      obs_times = c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24, 36, 48, 72, 96, 120, 168, 240, 336))
  sim <- rxode2::rxSolve(rxode2::zeroRe(ui), ev, returnType = "data.frame", maxsteps = 500000L)
  data.frame(treatment = paste(sub("_", ", ", lab$key), lab$route), id = 1L,
             time = sim$time, Cc = sim$Cc, dose = lab$dose * wt)
}))
conc_obj <- PKNCA::PKNCAconc(nca_sims |> filter(!is.na(Cc)), Cc ~ time | treatment + id)
dose_df <- nca_sims |> distinct(treatment, id, dose) |> mutate(time = 0)
dose_obj <- PKNCA::PKNCAdose(dose_df, dose ~ time | treatment + id)
intervals <- data.frame(start = 0, end = Inf, cmax = TRUE, tmax = TRUE, aucinf.obs = TRUE,
                        half.life = TRUE)
nca_res <- PKNCA::pk.nca(PKNCA::PKNCAdata(conc_obj, dose_obj, intervals = intervals))
as.data.frame(nca_res) |>
  filter(PPTESTCD %in% c("cmax", "tmax", "aucinf.obs", "half.life")) |>
  select(treatment, PPTESTCD, PPORRES) |>
  mutate(PPORRES = signif(PPORRES, 3)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = PPTESTCD, values_from = PPORRES) |>
  rename("Model and route" = treatment, "Cmax (mg/L)" = cmax, "Tmax (h)" = tmax,
         "AUC0-inf (mg*h/L)" = aucinf.obs, "t1/2 (h)" = half.life) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

# Assumptions and deviations

* **Equations from the deposited code.** Supplementary Equations S1-S16 give
  the structure only by example (the kidney stands for every tissue) and do
  not write out the plasma compartment or the metabolite submodel. The
  packaged ODEs are a line-by-line translation of the authors' mrgsolve code
  (`GenPBPK.R`), which the known-answer check above reproduces exactly.
* **Plasma state.** As in the code, the intravenous dose and the injection-site
  absorption enter the state the code calls `APlas_free`, which carries the
  whole plasma mass balance, while the reported total plasma concentration is
  `CPlas_free / Free`, i.e. `plasma / (v_plasma * fu)`. Tissue uptake is
  `Q * CPlas * Free`. This is kept exactly, because the fitted parameters were
  calibrated against it.
* **Blood and plasma volume.** Table 2 labels VPC as the plasma volume
  fraction, but the code uses it as the blood volume and takes
  `plasma = blood * (1 - Htc)`. The packaged models follow the code.
* **Swine flunixin Kim and Kabs.** Table 4 and the calibration script give
  Kim = 1 /h and Kabs = 0.4 /h; the figure and web-application code (which
  produced Figures 5 and 6, Supplementary Figure 1 and Table 5) use 0.5 /h and
  1.9 /h. The packaged model follows Table 4 and the calibration, under which
  the other swine flunixin parameters were fitted; the effect on the
  withdrawal intervals is shown above.
* **Swine florfenicol Kabs.** Table 4 prints 1.9 /h (Yang 2019), but both the
  calibration and the figure code use 0.4 /h, and with 0.4 /h the code
  reproduces the authors' saved calibration predictions to within 0.01%
  (1.9 /h gives early oral concentrations about 20% higher). The packaged
  model uses 0.4 /h.
* **Cattle florfenicol PM, PM1 and Kabs.** The calibration script used the in
  silico PM = 1.53, PM1 = 0.27 and Kabs = 0.4 /h; Table 3 and the figure code
  give 1.33, 0.90 and 1.9 /h (1.91 in the code). The packaged model uses the
  Table 3 values.
* **Penicillin G metabolite submodel.** The paper says penicillin G
  metabolism is a first-order loss "without monitoring the distribution of its
  specific metabolites", but the code runs the metabolite submodel for
  penicillin G too, with mrgsolve default parameters (PL1 10.52, PK1 4,
  PM1 0.5, PRest1 8, KurineC1 = KbileC1 = 0.1 L/h/kg, and fR1 0.5 in cattle and
  0.634 in swine), and Supplementary Equation S13 returns its biliary
  excretion to the gut as parent. That recycling roughly doubles late liver
  and kidney residues in cattle, so it is kept, with the defaults the figure
  code used. None of these values is in the paper.
* **Code-only values.** The swine flunixin metabolite parameters
  (PL1 9.26, PK1 4, PM1 1.57, PRest1 5, fR1 0.01) and the gastric emptying
  constant GE = 0.182 /h for every model are in the code but not in the
  paper's tables.
* **Precision.** Fitted values are carried at the precision of the deposited
  `Fit_*.rds` files; Tables 3 and 4 round or truncate them (for example cattle
  florfenicol fR 0.797 is printed 0.79 and swine florfenicol PL1 14.80 is
  printed 14.7). Literature values printed rounded in the tables use the
  code's value where it is consistent with the rounding (cattle florfenicol
  Kim 0.1618, Ksc 0.128, Kdissim 0.0104; Kabs 1.91; swine florfenicol Kdisssc
  0.0054; swine penicillin G PF 0.249). Molecular weights are those of Table 3
  (the code uses 296.24 / 312.24 for flunixin and 358.21 / 247.28 for
  florfenicol); only their ratio enters the model and it differs by less than
  0.02%.
* **Flunixin Frac.** Flunixin has no dissolution step (Tables 3 and 4 leave
  Frac and Kdiss blank and the code sets Frac = 1), but the authors' Monte
  Carlo still samples Frac (normal, CV 10%). The packaged flunixin models keep
  that as an IM / SC bioavailability factor with fixed variance.
* **Monte Carlo variability.** The coefficients of variation are the authors'
  assumptions, fixed in `ini()`: Table 2 SD / mean for physiology (including
  hematocrit, where the code instead uses CV 10%), 30% for the rest-of-body
  flow and volume, 20% for partition coefficients, 30% for rate constants and
  clearances and 10% for unbound fractions and Frac. Only the parameters the
  authors' code samples carry an eta; for penicillin G that excludes the
  metabolite partition coefficients and clearances. The truncation at the
  2.5th / 97.5th percentiles and the mean-preserving log-normal cannot be
  encoded in `ini()`; the normal etas are clamped at +/-1.96 SD in `model()`
  so that a plain `rxSolve()` cannot produce a negative volume, and the
  vignette draws the etas itself to match the authors exactly.
* **Table 5.** The current deposited figure code measures withdrawal intervals
  from the end of the last dosing interval and does not reproduce Table 5. An
  earlier snapshot in the same repository (`02032022_FARAD_Code`, same
  parameters, `set.seed(123)`), which measures them from the time of the last
  dose and rounds up, regenerates Table 5 when the maintainers ran it: 38 of
  the 42 label and extralabel entries exactly and the other four (all swine)
  within one day. This vignette uses that definition.
* **No residual-error model.** The authors fitted by weighted least squares
  and report none; `propSd` is a fixed placeholder.
* **Tolerances.** Kidney uses the liver tolerance (no kidney tolerances
  exist); penicillin G in swine uses the 0.025 ug/g minimum level of
  applicability because its US tolerance is zero (Chou 2022 Methods).
